title: Giving without resting on anything (section 4)
hookLine: give without dwelling on the gift, and the merit is boundless as space

cards: A birthday present goes out in the mail. A few days later, the sender feels a small itch: did it arrive? Did they like it?
Why haven't they said anything? The gift has left their hands, but part of them is still holding the string.
The Diamond Sutra, in its fourth section, takes up giving, the first of the perfections, and asks what happens if you cut the string completely.
Its answer reaches for the biggest picture it can find: the sky in every direction.

teach.h: GIVE, AND DON'T LEAN ON IT.
teach.b: First, the instruction. The Buddha tells Subhuti that a bodhisattva should give a gift without resting on anything. Not resting on the thing given.

Not on sights, sounds, smells, tastes, things touched, or things thought. Give, and don't lean your weight on the gift, or on the idea of it, or on the picture of yourself giving it. Second, the question about space.
Then the Buddha asks: Subhuti, is it easy to measure the space to the east? No, Subhuti says. And to the south, the west, the north, below, above, and every direction between?
No, each time. The question repeats, direction after direction, until the listener is standing in the middle of an open sky. Third, the point.
In the same way, the Buddha says, the merit of a bodhisattva who gives without resting on anything is not easy to measure. Yesterday the sutra said keep no count of beings.
Today it says the merit of that kind of giving can't be counted either. Let go of the counting, and what's left is too large to count.

Space doesn't keep anything. Sunlight, birds, a thrown ball pass through it, and it isn't any smaller afterward. A gift that rests on nothing is like that: it goes out and doesn't come back on a string.
Some readers find this hard, because noticing a gift is human, and a thank-you is a kindness too. The sutra doesn't forbid the thank-you. It asks the giver not to wait for it.

how: In Mahayana practice, giving is the first of the perfections, and section 4 of the Diamond Sutra is studied as its deepest form: a gift given without resting on the object, the receiver or the giver.

games.q: what does “giving without resting on anything” mean?
o: a gift given without leaning on the gift, the thanks or the giver
giving away everything you own and keeping nothing at all
giving only to people who could never pay you back

games.q: boundless as space: tap the pairs.
p: on the gift, or the idea of it

s: the Diamond Sutra says giving without resting on anything earns no merit
it says the merit is not easy to measure, like space in every direction.
the Buddha asks Subhuti about space in every direction, one at a time
east, south, west, north, below, above and between; no, each time.
the sutra forbids saying thank you for a gift
it asks the giver not to lean on the gift or wait for thanks; it forbids nothing about thanking.

games.q: the Buddha asks you: is it easy to measure the space to the east? what does Subhuti say?
games.why: no, and no again for every direction. so too, the Buddha says, the merit of giving that rests on nothing is not easy to measure.

practice: Choose something small you could give, a note, a compliment, your full attention for five minutes, and picture handing it over and opening your hand.

Feel the hand empty, then let your attention drift out in every direction, east, west, north, south, above, below, as far as the sky goes. When the thought of the gift returns, let it pass through, like a bird.

wordCard.voice: Giving without resting on anything. A gift that leans on nothing, not the object, not the thanks, not the giver, and merit that, like space, can't be measured. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: not resting, not standing on anything; the Diamond Sutra's word for how to give.

carryVoice: Your line: boundless as space. A gift with no string left on it. Tomorrow, not seen by marks.
